findings.recommendation: The pattern requires a literal `@`, so `logInfo("GET /reset?email=ada%40example.org")` writes the full address to the logs kept 90 days by the hosting provider (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), Art. 25). Request paths and query strings are the typical place this encoding appears. Also match `%40` (case-insensitive) as the separator, or decode URL-encoded text before masking, and add a test with an encoded address.
findings.title: Percent-encoded addresses reach the logs unmasked

findings.recommendation: The local-part class is ASCII-only: `用户@example.cn` has no matching character before `@` and is logged in full, and `élodie@example.fr` becomes `él***@example.fr`, leaking a character the mask meant to hide. Internationalized addresses (RFC 6531) are e-mail addresses the proposal promises to mask. Use a Unicode-aware class (`[\p{L}\p{N}._%+-]` with the `u` flag) for the local part and the domain, and add a test for it.
findings.title: Addresses with a non-ASCII local part are not masked

findings.recommendation: Only values are masked; a field keyed by an address, such as `logInfo("attempts", { [email]: count })`, logs the address in full. Mask the key too: `safe[maskEmails(key)] = …`.
findings.title: Field names are written to the log without masking

findings.recommendation: The mask keeps the first letter and the full domain. With a personal or small-company domain (`a***@lovelace.name`), the masked value still points at one person, so the logs keep personal data (GDPR Art. 4(1), Art. 5(1)(c)). Depends on the customers' domains, which the review could not see; if that matters, mask the domain too or log an opaque identifier instead.
findings.title: The kept domain can identify the person
